fields.title: Grace For Grace
fields.description: In this powerful book, Watchman Nee uses parables like the Prodigal Son to address deep questions about grace. Through relatable scenarios, he shows how grace is vital in our journey with Christ, reminding us of the abundant grace God has already made available for us to overcome sin and experience true freedom in Him.

fields.title: Parables of the New and the Old
fields.body_html:
Jesus' purpose was to call sinners to repentance, not the righteous. He explained that the law represents sin but cannot save. He emphasized the need for a new mindset, and His message and grace required transformation. The law shows people their sin, but only through Jesus' grace can they be healed.

After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And He said to him, Follow me. And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? And Jesus answered them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance. (Luke 5:27-30) “And they said to him, “The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.” And Jesus said to them, “Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’ (Luke 5:31-39) “No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made. Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.”(Matthew 9:16-17) One time, the Lord traveled and came to a certain place, where He saw Matthew (also known as Levi) sitting at the tax office. He called Levi, saying, “Follow me,” and the latter arose and followed the Lord. Suppose a stranger asked us to follow him. Would we get up and follow him? Of course not. Yet here is a Man to whom Matthew is drawn as iron to a magnet: he cannot help but forsake his former life, wealth, and all, to follow Him. Who knows the power behind Jesus’ words that causes Matthew to renounce his sinful life and abandon everything? Here is a Man that whoever sees Him must repent and be saved, that whoever listens to His voice receives a new life, that whoever hears His call rises up to follow Him.

Now, after Matthew had responded to the Lord’s call, he prepared a banquet and invited Jesus.

He also invited many publicans and sinners to come and dine with them. While they were at the table eating, certain Pharisees and their scribes murmured. They could not understand why the Lord Jesus and His disciples would have liked to eat and drink with publicans and sinners! Since they feared to question the Lord face to face, they complained to His disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with the publicans and sinners?” The disciples could not answer them, perhaps because they themselves did not understand why their Master would do such a thing.

When the Lord Jesus heard about it, He replied: “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.” This is the purpose of His coming to the world. He does not lower His standards by attending a banquet at a tax collector’s house, nor does He eat with tax collectors and sinners by accident. He comes with a clear aim. He says, “I have not…..but….” This explains the reason for His coming. His incarnation has a specific purpose. Whether He walks or heals, everything He does is purposeful. He never acts casually or speaks carelessly; His entire life is disciplined and planned. Therefore, His words here carried this meaning: You think I associate with publicans and sinners simply because I was invited to eat with them, yet in reality, this is the very reason I came from heaven: to call sinners to repentance. This is my purpose, and I have not deviated from my original plan.

Reason for the Parables “And Jesus answered them, “And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.’’ (Mark 2:17). Why does He say this? Because many people do not understand the purpose of the law. We should know that God gives the law not for men to keep but rather for them to know that they cannot keep it.

“Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.” (Galatians 3:19) God already knows men have sinned, and yet people themselves do not know they have sinned. Therefore, God gives the law to cause men to know themselves and to know that they cannot keep the law. Surely our Lord knows all about this.

It is very unimaginable that the Son of God would come into the world to teach people to uphold a law they are incapable of keeping, especially one that was introduced because of wrongdoing. Since the law cannot prevent people from sinning, would the Son of God come to tell them to do the impossible? God sent His Son to save humanity, so the Son does not demand that they keep the law as a condition for their salvation. God sent His Son to the world that the world might be saved through Him.

We are all sick people. How then, will God deal with us? He has two steps. First, He causes us to know that we are sick; and second, He induces us to seek for a physician. Suppose, for example, a person has tuberculosis but refuses to acknowledge it. He argues, “How can I have tuberculosis when I feel healthy?” You try to convince him that his daily symptoms suggest he may be in the early stages of tuberculosis, and if he doesn't seek treatment now, it will be harder to cure as the disease progresses. However, he insists that he doesn't have tuberculosis. Does his denial mean he doesn't have tuberculosis? Not at all. His denial simply shows that he refuses to acknowledge the reality of his condition, which could eventually make the tuberculosis incurable.

The same is true with our salvation. The problem is not because God has no way to save us, the problem lies instead in people’s not knowing and acknowledging that they are sinners. For this reason, God first gives the law to men to cause them to see that they are indeed sinners. The law gives us the knowledge of sin; it also causes us to know ourselves. Although the law cannot ever make us just, nor can it save us. The order of salvation, therefore, is first, God gives us the law, then He sends the Lord Jesus as grace to the world. When a physician examines a patient, he first diagnoses the disease and next he writes out a prescription.

God gives the law that people might know they are sinners; He then sends grace, meaning He sends the Lord Jesus, that they might be healed. To those who are so stiff-necked as to say they are not sick, that they have no sin, to them the Lord Jesus declares: “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.” What He means to say here is this: “I will have to let you self-righteous people continue to keep the law and be Pharisees.”

People must receive the first help before they can receive the second. If they are not willing to accept the witness of the law, they will not be able to receive the help of grace and truth. Formerly I thought I was fine; but after the physician has felt my pulse and measured my temperature and carefully examined me, tells me I am a sick man. Formerly I considered myself a good man, but now I meet the law which tells me I am a sinner. The work of the law is to show people that they are sick with sin.

“They that are in good health have no need of a physician; but they that are sick.” This is a basic principle. Are you sick? Do you have some hidden illness you cannot tell others about? Do you have in your heart some secret sins which are undetected by men? Let me say outright that God knows all hidden illness and secret sins. He will touch those who have them. How pitiful it is for a person to know very well how naked he is before God and to know very well how he participates in unclean sins, and yet attempts to hide and to cover and to reform himself before he believes in Christ. Such a person can be compared to one who waits till he gets well before he will send for a physician. What a foolish way of thinking and acting! Only when a person honestly acknowledges he is a sinner will he ever be healed.

“Just as I am, I come, I come!” The words of this well-known hymn were written by a sister in the Lord when she was only twenty years of age. From childhood she had a sense of sin. She often asked herself how a person like her could ever see God’s face. She frequented many churches and met many pastors. She asked them what she would do in order to be saved. Many told her, Wait till you are somehow better and then believe in the Lord Jesus. Some people advised her to pray and read the Bible more often. Others encouraged her to do more good. This continued on for about seven or eight years but the result was that she was actually getting worse and not better. Finally, she met an old preacher of the gospel. She asked him “What must I do to be brought close to God and be saved?” This old man gently laid his hand on her shoulder and replied, “Just as you are, go and meet God.” She exclaimed in response, “Do you really think I don’t need to be reformed and become better before I can believe in the Lord Jesus?”

The old man answered, “Indeed, you don’t need too, and you can come just as you are.” From that day forward, she began to understand that she could come to the Lord just as she was. And so this lady brought her sickness to the Physician sent by God and she was healed. On reaching home, she wrote this hymn: “Just as I am . . . I come, I come!”

What is grace? Grace is, that just as I am I can come to the Lord. For the Lord Jesus wants sinners to come to Him just as they are. Now as Jesus answered the Pharisees in this way, they immediately came up with another question. Disregarding the matter of whether they were sick or well, they accused the Lord and His disciples of being excessive eaters: “And they said to him, “The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.” (Luke 5:33) Note that fasting here is mentioned in contrast to feasting. Their words had a double meaning: First, we fast twice a week “I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.”(Luke 18:12) but your disciples eat seven days a week. This is the surface meaning.

Second, we are not like your disciples who just eat and drink. We are good at religious practices, we have done what ordinary people find hard to do. Some people see being vegetarian as a virtue, but the Pharisees believe they are even more virtuous because they choose not to eat at all. Whatever good deeds common people cannot do, these Pharisees will do in order to obtain the reputation of being Godly.

Since their question had this double meaning, the Lord Jesus answered them separately. He first answered the surface question. “And Jesus said to them, “Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.”(Luke 5:34-35) What Jesus meant was: “If I as the bridegroom am present, the sons of the bride-groom do not need to fast.” This explains why His disciples were not fasting, since the Lord Jesus had not been taken away. Though when He is taken away, then His disciples would fast. Before the Lord is rejected by men and crucified, the disciples do not need to fast. This answers the question concerning the matter of fasting at its surface level.

The Lord then used certain parables explaining the incompatibility between the new and the old as His answer to the deeper root question regarding fasting. Though why did He use these parables as his mode of reply? It will help us to understand Jesus’ use of His parables here if we keep clearly in mind that the Pharisees’ mindset was that they had to continually be doing good, that they had to have good deeds in religion and keep the laws and commandments of God with all their strength in order to please Him.

The Lord used these parables with a view to show the Pharisees that the things which He brought to the world were totally separate from the rituals and ordinances of the law and that the grace which He brought in was wholly different from the law. The purpose of these parables was therefore to show that law and grace cannot be mixed together. For if they were mixed up, law would no longer be law and grace would no longer be grace. With this understanding, let us look into these parables concerning the new and the old which were spoken by the Lord.

Using a New Cloth to Fix an Old Garment “No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made.” (Matthew 9:16) Here, our Lord shows us the parable of using a piece of new cloth to mend an old cloth. Such a thing is commonly done, yet the Lord points out its incompatibility. If a piece of new cloth is put on an old garment, this new cloth will make a worse patch to the garment. In the Bible, the word garment stands for our righteousness before God. When the garment is torn, the shame of the flesh is exposed. We may think we are well dressed, but there is One who sees us just as we are, whether in the dark or in the light. God declares that our garment is torn and that there is no way to cover up our sins and shame. Our history is so full of uncleanness and sins that we cannot share these things with others. We may keep such matters hidden in our hearts, but we cannot hide them from God. And so the immediate problem is not in proving whether or not this garment is torn, rather it is in proposing what to do to this old and torn garment. Naturally, our own way would be to mend it.

Unfinished fabric does not refer to new cloth as opposed to old cloth. It refers to cloth that hasn't been tightened yet because the manufacturing process is not finished. Patching an old garment with this kind of cloth will rip the old garment even more. Spiritually speaking, let it be understood that what many people receive is not the finished work of Christ. They accept the outward name or trademark, but they have not accepted the finished work of Christ on the cross. If they are asked who Jesus Christ is, they will say He is a great moralist, a great religious leader, or a perfect model for us to imitate. Such words are spoken by people who do not believe in the precious blood of our Lord. This is exactly what unfinished fabric signifies.

Some people say that Jesus was not born of the Virgin Mary, that He is not the Son of God, that His shedding of blood was not for the atoning of sin, that He was not risen from the dead, that His words and deeds before His death serve only as examples to us, and that His death has nothing to do with us. They consider the works of the Lord Jesus during His thirty-three years of living on earth as enough for them; they have not seen the necessity for the Son of man to be lifted up in death, “And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,” ( John 3:14). They take the death of the Lord Jesus as simply the murder of an ordinary person. They do not see His death as God having died for us. They have never realized that if the Lord had not died, we would all have to die. In short, they accept the teachings of the Lord Jesus as “undressed cloth.” By cutting a piece out of it, they use it to patch their old and torn garment of unrighteousness. Even though some may not voice these words, they conceive such thoughts in their heart.

At one point, a brother in the Lord gave a copy of the New Testament to another person. After the latter had read the Four Gospels, he declared that he must learn from Jesus because his conduct was not as perfect as that of Jesus. Though in doing this, he did not acknowledge himself to be a sinner. Such a concept does not prevail only among the unbelievers; it can also be found among the so-called Christians. If you were to ask such a person if his conduct is as good as that of the Lord Jesus, his answer would be an unhesitating no. Yet if you were to further ask him what he was going to do about it, he would say that he would give more money to the church and would do more good. On the one hand, he confesses that his garment is torn, though on the other hand, he thinks of cutting a piece of new cloth and patching up the old garment with it. Yet our Lord states clearly that if a new cloth is used to mend an old garment, it will tear the garment and make the patch worse.

Some people may reason: My garment is torn, I am a sinner before God, and therefore I must fast twice a week. Others may wonder: My garment is torn, what shall I do? I know. I will take from my monthly income to offer to the church. Or still others may think: I have sinned, what shall I do? I will get up early in the morning to read a chapter of the Bible on my knees.

People always conclude that since they have sinned, they must do these or other things to mend their ways. It is like patching up an old garment with piece after piece of undressed cloth. However, the decision of the Lord Jesus is that in so doing, a worse tear is made. The more you repair, the worse the tear. You may perhaps speculate that nothing of this sort will ever happen, but the fact is, it does happen. For example, someone may be prone to lying. He is determined not to lie again. So, he decides to draw a dark circle in his diary if he lies. The result is that there are more dark circles in his diary than he ever could have imagined. How true is it that the outcome of mending is to cause the tear to be far worse and more evident to everybody? (I am not saying people should not fast, read the Bible, give offerings, and so forth. I am simply explaining how futile it is if we try to use these things as merits to mend our weaknesses and to obtain God’s favor.)

Using a New Garment to Mend an Old Garment The picture Luke draws for us is different from that painted by Matthew and Mark. Luke’s account says: “He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.” (Luke 5:36) If a man has two garments, one new and one old, and he cuts a piece from the new garment and puts it on the old, when he sees the old garment is torn, he will be called by everybody a fool. No one would ever do such a thing materially, but odd to say, many always do exactly the same spiritually. The new cloth which both Matthew and Mark mention is undressed cloth which points to the Lord Jesus before His death, that is to say, before His work is done.

When He died and after His work was done, He cried out at the cross, “It is finished.” His death meant the accomplishment of the work of redemption, whereas His life is like an undressed cloth. The cloth Luke writes about in his Gospel is not undressed cloth but finished cloth. If anyone attempts to use the finished cloth of the Lord Jesus to mend his torn garment, he will try to do his best and in addition ask the Lord Jesus to help him where he lacks. Some Christians maintain that we must keep the Ten Commandments. If they are asked if they have kept them, their response would be that for what they can't do, they will ask the Lord Jesus for help. Yet the Lord himself declares that no one rends a piece from a new garment and puts it upon an old torn garment. We cannot do well, therefore it is better to throw away the old altogether and put on the new garment.

We have no way to save ourselves except by confessing our sins. There is no way to get rid of our sins and gain God’s favor except to cut off the self-styled good of the flees, those old rags of ours and acknowledge the Lord Jesus Christ as our Savior and to trust in His completed work of redemption on the cross. Having been crucified, He has already satisfied the righteous demand of God. The robe which He offers to us is new and whole. Nothing needs to be added to it, for on the cross the Lord declares that “it is finished. “Many do not know that the work of redemption is already done. They are still thinking that if they are to be saved they must at least do some good otherwise how can they be saved? Yet they do not realize that such a thought is as foolish as presenting a piece of a new garment to put upon an old garment.

The Bible does not tell us to improve ourselves, since the Lord has already done it all. Jesus Christ has borne our sins on the cross and there He said “It is finished.” He has completed the work and nothing is therefore left to be done. Today we do not need to do anything except to confess that our garment is torn, that we are corrupted and are unable to do any good, and to ask Him to give us a new garment.

However, if you want to excel, you will have to do it repeatedly. You ought to know that aside from trusting the redemption which the Lord Jesus has accomplished once and for all, there is no other way of salvation. “No man rips a piece from a new garment and puts it upon an old garment or else he will rip the new, and also the piece from the new will not match with the old.” To tear the new means to destroy the finished work of Jesus Christ.

Additionally, the new and the old will never agree. For instance, if you take a piece of a new, white garment and put it on an old, black garment, the difference in colors will be instantly noticeable. To mend something it requires a certain compatibility between materials. By placing a piece of a new garment on an old one, the disparity in colors will immediately reveal the wear and tear. This is like telling people how unfit things are. Let us be reminded that the salvation which God gives to us, as represented by a new garment, is totally different from our old garment.

Are you thinking of filling in what you lack with the Lord Jesus? This is totally unacceptable. If you believe in the Lord Jesus, then you must accept a brand new garment. If you take only a little of the new garment, you will look even worse. Today we have a new garment, which is the righteousness of God. If you wholly accept the Lord, the righteousness of God will cover all your shame and nakedness. However, if you contemplate taking only a piece from the new garment, which is the righteousness of God, and putting it on your old garment, this will only serve to expose your own ugliness.

The teaching of Jesus Christ is like unfinished cloth; therefore, it cannot save us. It is His finished work of redemption that saves us. Yet we cannot tear a piece from His garment of redemption to put on our ragged conduct. We can only take off completely what we consider our best conduct and put on the new garment of righteousness given by God. For God wants us to throw away our rags and to be clothed with His new garment. What man has is a ragged garment, but thank God for what He has is a new garment. There is no reason for man to refuse this new garment? Hallelujah!

The redemption of Jesus Christ is sufficient for every person’s salvation. If any man is not saved, it is not because there is no new garment nor because he does not know how to mend his old garment but because he refuses to be clothed with the new garment. On the other hand, a person is saved not because he has good conduct, but because he believes and accepts the finished work of the Lord Jesus. Whether one is saved or not does not depend on his past as a good man or a bad man but entirely depends upon whether he accepts or rejects the redemption of the Lord.

All who are willing to receive Jesus Christ shall be saved. “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.” (John 3:16) Hallelujah! This is a fact. The Son of God already died, and the new garment is also available. All you need is to be willing to put it on. Praise the Lord! The problem with salvation is not how valuable our conduct is but how valuable the cross of Calvary is. In this matter of salvation, our conduct has no merit at all; it’s the death of the Lord Jesus on the cross that is meritorious.

The New Wine “Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.” (Matthew 9:17). The “Garment” points to the external work of the gospel, for it is visible to men. The “New wine” refers to the internal work of the gospel because it is invisible to men. The gospel of God includes two aspects: first, to make Christ our righteousness so that we may live before God in this righteousness.

Nothing needs to be added because Christ has already become the righteousness of God; it is therefore impossible to add anything to it. Not because our good conduct has pleased God, but simply because Christ died and resurrected. Being in Christ, we are looked upon by God as acceptable to Him as Christ himself. We are saved not because we are different from other people, but because we are in Christ. Being in Christ, we can approach God. Having been clothed with Christ, we can live before God and please Him.

The second aspect of the gospel is for Christ to live in us that we may live before the world.

According to the spirit, we live before God; according to the flesh, we live in this world. “Garment” tells of how God gives us Christ and has made Him to be our righteousness so that we may live before God. “Wine” speaks of how God gives us Christ and has made Him to be our life and power that we may accept His control and by Him live before men. Some people complain, saying, “Indeed, I am saved and have received forgiveness of sins before God, but my daily life is still the same as before. What can I do about it?” Please remember that God has not only clothed you outwardly with a new garment in order to cover and adorn you, He has also put inside you a power like that of the new wine which will dissolve all the old things. We should know that salvation has this double aspect: that of the objective which is before God, and that of the subjective which is within us.

In other words, there is justification on the one hand and regeneration on the other. It is absolutely impossible to be regenerated and not be justified, or justified without being regenerated. Justification obtains for us a new position before God, whereas regeneration gives us a new life. Some people pay attention only to justification without so much as considering this aspect of regeneration, yet other people overemphasise regeneration and overlook justification. Due to their misconception, none of these people realize that regeneration and justification co-occur, and they can hold such prejudiced views. Actually, justification and regeneration balance each other well. In the third chapter of the Gospel of John, the word “must” occurs several times. We will focus on two of them. In verse 7, “Do not marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born again.”(John 3:7) “And as Moses lifted the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted,” (John 3:14). The same word in Greek is used in both cases. What is said in verse 14 is objective, for the Lord Jesus is lifted that we may receive the forgiveness of sins and be justified. What is stated in verse 7 is subjective, as it promises us new life. Being justified, we have liberty before God; having been regenerated, we have a new life within us.

Some people may speculate within themselves, thinking, “I am very much afraid to approach God because I do not know if He will save me or not.” They believe, won’t God say to me, ‘Depart from me, you wicked one!’ I am a sinner, I do not know whether God wants me or not.” To such people we would say: Do not be afraid, for the Lord Jesus has already come and has died for our sins. He has already satisfied God’s justice, and He has also been resurrected. Today, all who come to God through the Lord Jesus Christ shall be saved. The Lord himself has assured us that “Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God.” (John 3:18) Paul also declared that “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Acts 13:39). You who trust in the Lord today are justified. You ought to know that through Him you can come before God with a conscience free of fear because “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” (Romans 8:1) You know you are saved. Yet, you feel miserable because you want to do what is good, but you cannot carry it out. “For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out.” (Romans 7:18) You have seen changes in the lives of other believers, yet in yourself you see no change. You are saved as much as they are; why then are there changes in them but none in you? Why is your life not much different from what you were before? You cry over your defeats and weaknesses. You think over the matter of your salvation.

You have to acknowledge that you are saved and that you have eternal life; but being the kind of person as you are, you ask yourself if you are really saved because you can hardly believe so. Therefore, you try hard er to do good, to pray, and to read the Bible more, and to discipline yourself more strictly in order to please God. You seem to see some results in three or five days, yet the effect is all in vain when measured by months or years. This is exactly what the Lord Jesus meant when He said we must not mend the old garment with a piece from the new garment; that after being saved, we ought to use the new wine, the power of this new life to overcome all outward entanglements. The new wine is put within us to give us new life and the power of living.

All who are justified are regenerated. Whoever has the new garment also has the new wine.

Hallelujah! God has already put this regenerated life in us; henceforth we are new men. The new wine is the power of the gospel. We have this power in us, causing us to live a victorious life.

Now the question is, where is the new wine to be put?

The New Wine-skins and the Old Wine-skins “Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.”(Matthew 9:17) Why should the new wine not be put into old wine-skins? (According to Jewish custom, wine is put into skins) It is because the new wine has tremendous power of expansion. It will burst the old wine-skin if it is put into it, and then the wine will be spilled.

What is the meaning of the old wine-skins? Some people say that the old wine-skins represent us but this kind of interpretation is not correct. Since the old garment does not stand for us, how can the old wineskins represent us? We ought to consider the context of these words. As the old garment points to the so called self-righteousness of men, so the old wine-skins refers to our natural good conduct. This old wineskin is related to fasting in the preceding passage. Fasting enables us to boast that we are not like the tax-collector since we fast twice a week. What causes us to boast before God is the old wine-skins. Old wine-skins speaks of both the better conduct we consider ourselves as having had before we were saved as well as the good works which we may depend on after we are saved.

As Christians, we may turn back like the Galatian believers and think of pleasing God by keeping the law. We try to rely on our own strength to obtain His favor. This is what Paul observed in the third chapter of Galatians: “Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3). All who begin with the Lord Jesus and then try to be perfected by themselves are putting new wine into old wine-skins. In the past to date, no one has been able to mix Christianity and Judaism and still preserve both. The result of such a mixture can only cause Christianity to be unlike Christianity and Judaism to be unlike Judaism.

Both will lose their original flavor. God will not tolerate such a thing. The Roman church has combined Judaism with Christianity. On the one hand, they adopt the customs and rituals of the Old Covenant; on the other hand, they embrace the name of the New Covenant. Is this Christianity? No. Is this Judaism? The answer is equally no. Add Judaism to Christianity and the result is neither Judaism nor Christianity. The new wine can only be put into fresh wineskins. Only then can it be powerful and effective.

The new wine must follow the principle of the New Covenant, and then it will please God. Having this new wine in you, you have a power within that can control you. If you are not saved, you will not have such an experience, and neither will you change. However, if you are saved, you will always sense within you a law that is in control of you. There was a mother who was very careful in speech, but she had a very talkative son. Whenever they visited their relatives, the mother would pull his sleeves to signal that he should stop talking because he had already said enough. Yet during the conversation, her son would talk constantly and completely ignore his mother’s pulling of his sleeve.

How marvelous it is for a Christian that when he goes out alone with no one at his side and becomes too talkative, he feels within him a person pulling him, saying, That is enough. For if he continues to speak, he will be ungodly and unlike a Christian. As soon as he listens to the inner voice and stops talking, he experiences peace. What is this? This is the new wine. Can we put new wine into old wineskins? No, it is right to inscribe the words of the Bible upon our hearts, but to write them on the wall is like putting them into old wine-skins. In other words, this is an attempt to uphold the law through our own efforts.

The law of the Old Covenant is external, while that of the New Covenant is internal. Here is the difference between the New Covenant and the Old. Just as the people under the Old Covenant could not, in themselves, keep the Ten Commandments, so too Christians under the New Covenant cannot keep such external commandments either. The Old Covenant is inscribed on stone tablets, the words of which we in ourselves have no power to keep; but the New Covenant is written upon the heart, giving us strength to keep it. Thank God, we do not need words written on paper to remind us. We instead have one who reminds us from within. The new wine cannot be put into old wine-skins. The latest wine must be put into fresh wine-skins. God has not commanded us to keep the outward law, but He does command us to keep the inward law. For the law within us is living and not dead. “For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death.”(Romans 8:2) This law is in us, and it enables us to keep the law of God. We have not only the new garment outside, but also the new wine inside. We have not only righteousness but also new life. The latest wine is put into fresh wine-skins, that we may live in the newness of life.

The Old Wine “And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.” (Luke 5:39). This is the consensus of the world. All who have drunk the old wine will not desire the new. Yet, God will not give old wine to man to drink. The Jews rejected what the Lord Jesus gave to them because they had drunk too much of the old wine. How our minds, too, are drunk with old wine. We think that it will be well if we do well and improve ourselves.

In actual fact, however, if a person drinks only the old wine, there is no new power, no real explosive power in him. If he does not drink the new wine, he will be powerless year after year. He who thinks of pleasing God with his own good conduct is following a futile path. Only by trusting in the Lord Jesus Christ and drinking the new wine can a person please God.

Having studied these parables of the new and the old, we can now clearly understand that there is absolutely no way to mix up law and grace. Let us never for a moment try to mend our rags with the righteousness of Christ, but simply put on Christ. Let us never think that we have to do good after we are saved; let us simply trust Christ as our life and let Him live Himself out through us.
fields.body_text: Jesus' purpose was to call sinners to repentance, not the righteous. He explained that the law represents sin but cannot save. He emphasized the need for a new mindset, and His message and grace required transformation. The law shows people their sin, but only through Jesus' grace can they be healed. After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And He said to him, Follow me. And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? And Jesus answered them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance. (Luke 5:27-30) “And they said to him, “The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.” And Jesus said to them, “Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’ (Luke 5:31-39) “No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made. Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.”(Matthew 9:16-17) One time, the Lord traveled and came to a certain place, where He saw Matthew (also known as Levi) sitting at the tax office. He called Levi, saying, “Follow me,” and the latter arose and followed the Lord. Suppose a stranger asked us to follow him. Would we get up and follow him? Of course not. Yet here is a Man to whom Matthew is drawn as iron to a magnet: he cannot help but forsake his former life, wealth, and all, to follow Him. Who knows the power behind Jesus’ words that causes Matthew to renounce his sinful life and abandon everything? Here is a Man that whoever sees Him must repent and be saved, that whoever listens to His voice receives a new life, that whoever hears His call rises up to follow Him. Now, after Matthew had responded to the Lord’s call, he prepared a banquet and invited Jesus. He also invited many publicans and sinners to come and dine with them. While they were at the table eating, certain Pharisees and their scribes murmured. They could not understand why the Lord Jesus and His disciples would have liked to eat and drink with publicans and sinners! Since they feared to question the Lord face to face, they complained to His disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with the publicans and sinners?” The disciples could not answer them, perhaps because they themselves did not understand why their Master would do such a thing. When the Lord Jesus heard about it, He replied: “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.” This is the purpose of His coming to the world. He does not lower His standards by attending a banquet at a tax collector’s house, nor does He eat with tax collectors and sinners by accident. He comes with a clear aim. He says, “I have not…..but….” This explains the reason for His coming. His incarnation has a specific purpose. Whether He walks or heals, everything He does is purposeful. He never acts casually or speaks carelessly; His entire life is disciplined and planned. Therefore, His words here carried this meaning: You think I associate with publicans and sinners simply because I was invited to eat with them, yet in reality, this is the very reason I came from heaven: to call sinners to repentance. This is my purpose, and I have not deviated from my original plan. Reason for the Parables “And Jesus answered them, “And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.’’ (Mark 2:17). Why does He say this? Because many people do not understand the purpose of the law. We should know that God gives the law not for men to keep but rather for them to know that they cannot keep it. “Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.” (Galatians 3:19) God already knows men have sinned, and yet people themselves do not know they have sinned. Therefore, God gives the law to cause men to know themselves and to know that they cannot keep the law. Surely our Lord knows all about this. It is very unimaginable that the Son of God would come into the world to teach people to uphold a law they are incapable of keeping, especially one that was introduced because of wrongdoing. Since the law cannot prevent people from sinning, would the Son of God come to tell them to do the impossible? God sent His Son to save humanity, so the Son does not demand that they keep the law as a condition for their salvation. God sent His Son to the world that the world might be saved through Him. We are all sick people. How then, will God deal with us? He has two steps. First, He causes us to know that we are sick; and second, He induces us to seek for a physician. Suppose, for example, a person has tuberculosis but refuses to acknowledge it. He argues, "How can I have tuberculosis when I feel healthy?" You try to convince him that his daily symptoms suggest he may be in the early stages of tuberculosis, and if he doesn't seek treatment now, it will be harder to cure as the disease progresses. However, he insists that he doesn't have tuberculosis. Does his denial mean he doesn't have tuberculosis? Not at all. His denial simply shows that he refuses to acknowledge the reality of his condition, which could eventually make the tuberculosis incurable. The same is true with our salvation. The problem is not because God has no way to save us, the problem lies instead in people’s not knowing and acknowledging that they are sinners. For this reason, God first gives the law to men to cause them to see that they are indeed sinners. The law gives us the knowledge of sin; it also causes us to know ourselves. Although the law cannot ever make us just, nor can it save us. The order of salvation, therefore, is first, God gives us the law, then He sends the Lord Jesus as grace to the world. When a physician examines a patient, he first diagnoses the disease and next he writes out a prescription. God gives the law that people might know they are sinners; He then sends grace, meaning He sends the Lord Jesus, that they might be healed. To those who are so stiff-necked as to say they are not sick, that they have no sin, to them the Lord Jesus declares: “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.” What He means to say here is this: “I will have to let you self-righteous people continue to keep the law and be Pharisees.” People must receive the first help before they can receive the second. If they are not willing to accept the witness of the law, they will not be able to receive the help of grace and truth. Formerly I thought I was fine; but after the physician has felt my pulse and measured my temperature and carefully examined me, tells me I am a sick man. Formerly I considered myself a good man, but now I meet the law which tells me I am a sinner. The work of the law is to show people that they are sick with sin. “They that are in good health have no need of a physician; but they that are sick.” This is a basic principle. Are you sick? Do you have some hidden illness you cannot tell others about? Do you have in your heart some secret sins which are undetected by men? Let me say outright that God knows all hidden illness and secret sins. He will touch those who have them. How pitiful it is for a person to know very well how naked he is before God and to know very well how he participates in unclean sins, and yet attempts to hide and to cover and to reform himself before he believes in Christ. Such a person can be compared to one who waits till he gets well before he will send for a physician. What a foolish way of thinking and acting! Only when a person honestly acknowledges he is a sinner will he ever be healed. “Just as I am, I come, I come!” The words of this well-known hymn were written by a sister in the Lord when she was only twenty years of age. From childhood she had a sense of sin. She often asked herself how a person like her could ever see God’s face. She frequented many churches and met many pastors. She asked them what she would do in order to be saved. Many told her, Wait till you are somehow better and then believe in the Lord Jesus. Some people advised her to pray and read the Bible more often. Others encouraged her to do more good. This continued on for about seven or eight years but the result was that she was actually getting worse and not better. Finally, she met an old preacher of the gospel. She asked him “What must I do to be brought close to God and be saved?” This old man gently laid his hand on her shoulder and replied, “Just as you are, go and meet God.” She exclaimed in response, “Do you really think I don’t need to be reformed and become better before I can believe in the Lord Jesus?” The old man answered, “Indeed, you don’t need too, and you can come just as you are.” From that day forward, she began to understand that she could come to the Lord just as she was. And so this lady brought her sickness to the Physician sent by God and she was healed. On reaching home, she wrote this hymn: “Just as I am . . . I come, I come!” What is grace? Grace is, that just as I am I can come to the Lord. For the Lord Jesus wants sinners to come to Him just as they are. Now as Jesus answered the Pharisees in this way, they immediately came up with another question. Disregarding the matter of whether they were sick or well, they accused the Lord and His disciples of being excessive eaters: “And they said to him, “The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.” (Luke 5:33) Note that fasting here is mentioned in contrast to feasting. Their words had a double meaning: First, we fast twice a week “I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.”(Luke 18:12) but your disciples eat seven days a week. This is the surface meaning. Second, we are not like your disciples who just eat and drink. We are good at religious practices, we have done what ordinary people find hard to do. Some people see being vegetarian as a virtue, but the Pharisees believe they are even more virtuous because they choose not to eat at all. Whatever good deeds common people cannot do, these Pharisees will do in order to obtain the reputation of being Godly. Since their question had this double meaning, the Lord Jesus answered them separately. He first answered the surface question. “And Jesus said to them, “Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.”(Luke 5:34-35) What Jesus meant was: “If I as the bridegroom am present, the sons of the bride-groom do not need to fast.” This explains why His disciples were not fasting, since the Lord Jesus had not been taken away. Though when He is taken away, then His disciples would fast. Before the Lord is rejected by men and crucified, the disciples do not need to fast. This answers the question concerning the matter of fasting at its surface level. The Lord then used certain parables explaining the incompatibility between the new and the old as His answer to the deeper root question regarding fasting. Though why did He use these parables as his mode of reply? It will help us to understand Jesus’ use of His parables here if we keep clearly in mind that the Pharisees’ mindset was that they had to continually be doing good, that they had to have good deeds in religion and keep the laws and commandments of God with all their strength in order to please Him. The Lord used these parables with a view to show the Pharisees that the things which He brought to the world were totally separate from the rituals and ordinances of the law and that the grace which He brought in was wholly different from the law. The purpose of these parables was therefore to show that law and grace cannot be mixed together. For if they were mixed up, law would no longer be law and grace would no longer be grace. With this understanding, let us look into these parables concerning the new and the old which were spoken by the Lord. Using a New Cloth to Fix an Old Garment “No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made.” (Matthew 9:16) Here, our Lord shows us the parable of using a piece of new cloth to mend an old cloth. Such a thing is commonly done, yet the Lord points out its incompatibility. If a piece of new cloth is put on an old garment, this new cloth will make a worse patch to the garment. In the Bible, the word garment stands for our righteousness before God. When the garment is torn, the shame of the flesh is exposed. We may think we are well dressed, but there is One who sees us just as we are, whether in the dark or in the light. God declares that our garment is torn and that there is no way to cover up our sins and shame. Our history is so full of uncleanness and sins that we cannot share these things with others. We may keep such matters hidden in our hearts, but we cannot hide them from God. And so the immediate problem is not in proving whether or not this garment is torn, rather it is in proposing what to do to this old and torn garment. Naturally, our own way would be to mend it. Unfinished fabric does not refer to new cloth as opposed to old cloth. It refers to cloth that hasn't been tightened yet because the manufacturing process is not finished. Patching an old garment with this kind of cloth will rip the old garment even more. Spiritually speaking, let it be understood that what many people receive is not the finished work of Christ. They accept the outward name or trademark, but they have not accepted the finished work of Christ on the cross. If they are asked who Jesus Christ is, they will say He is a great moralist, a great religious leader, or a perfect model for us to imitate. Such words are spoken by people who do not believe in the precious blood of our Lord. This is exactly what unfinished fabric signifies. Some people say that Jesus was not born of the Virgin Mary, that He is not the Son of God, that His shedding of blood was not for the atoning of sin, that He was not risen from the dead, that His words and deeds before His death serve only as examples to us, and that His death has nothing to do with us. They consider the works of the Lord Jesus during His thirty-three years of living on earth as enough for them; they have not seen the necessity for the Son of man to be lifted up in death, “And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,” ( John 3:14). They take the death of the Lord Jesus as simply the murder of an ordinary person. They do not see His death as God having died for us. They have never realized that if the Lord had not died, we would all have to die. In short, they accept the teachings of the Lord Jesus as “undressed cloth.” By cutting a piece out of it, they use it to patch their old and torn garment of unrighteousness. Even though some may not voice these words, they conceive such thoughts in their heart. At one point, a brother in the Lord gave a copy of the New Testament to another person. After the latter had read the Four Gospels, he declared that he must learn from Jesus because his conduct was not as perfect as that of Jesus. Though in doing this, he did not acknowledge himself to be a sinner. Such a concept does not prevail only among the unbelievers; it can also be found among the so-called Christians. If you were to ask such a person if his conduct is as good as that of the Lord Jesus, his answer would be an unhesitating no. Yet if you were to further ask him what he was going to do about it, he would say that he would give more money to the church and would do more good. On the one hand, he confesses that his garment is torn, though on the other hand, he thinks of cutting a piece of new cloth and patching up the old garment with it. Yet our Lord states clearly that if a new cloth is used to mend an old garment, it will tear the garment and make the patch worse. Some people may reason: My garment is torn, I am a sinner before God, and therefore I must fast twice a week. Others may wonder: My garment is torn, what shall I do? I know. I will take from my monthly income to offer to the church. Or still others may think: I have sinned, what shall I do? I will get up early in the morning to read a chapter of the Bible on my knees. People always conclude that since they have sinned, they must do these or other things to mend their ways. It is like patching up an old garment with piece after piece of undressed cloth. However, the decision of the Lord Jesus is that in so doing, a worse tear is made. The more you repair, the worse the tear. You may perhaps speculate that nothing of this sort will ever happen, but the fact is, it does happen. For example, someone may be prone to lying. He is determined not to lie again. So, he decides to draw a dark circle in his diary if he lies. The result is that there are more dark circles in his diary than he ever could have imagined. How true is it that the outcome of mending is to cause the tear to be far worse and more evident to everybody? (I am not saying people should not fast, read the Bible, give offerings, and so forth. I am simply explaining how futile it is if we try to use these things as merits to mend our weaknesses and to obtain God’s favor.) Using a New Garment to Mend an Old Garment The picture Luke draws for us is different from that painted by Matthew and Mark. Luke’s account says: “He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.” (Luke 5:36) If a man has two garments, one new and one old, and he cuts a piece from the new garment and puts it on the old, when he sees the old garment is torn, he will be called by everybody a fool. No one would ever do such a thing materially, but odd to say, many always do exactly the same spiritually. The new cloth which both Matthew and Mark mention is undressed cloth which points to the Lord Jesus before His death, that is to say, before His work is done. When He died and after His work was done, He cried out at the cross, “It is finished.” His death meant the accomplishment of the work of redemption, whereas His life is like an undressed cloth. The cloth Luke writes about in his Gospel is not undressed cloth but finished cloth. If anyone attempts to use the finished cloth of the Lord Jesus to mend his torn garment, he will try to do his best and in addition ask the Lord Jesus to help him where he lacks. Some Christians maintain that we must keep the Ten Commandments. If they are asked if they have kept them, their response would be that for what they can't do, they will ask the Lord Jesus for help. Yet the Lord himself declares that no one rends a piece from a new garment and puts it upon an old torn garment. We cannot do well, therefore it is better to throw away the old altogether and put on the new garment. We have no way to save ourselves except by confessing our sins. There is no way to get rid of our sins and gain God’s favor except to cut off the self-styled good of the flees, those old rags of ours and acknowledge the Lord Jesus Christ as our Savior and to trust in His completed work of redemption on the cross. Having been crucified, He has already satisfied the righteous demand of God. The robe which He offers to us is new and whole. Nothing needs to be added to it, for on the cross the Lord declares that “it is finished. “Many do not know that the work of redemption is already done. They are still thinking that if they are to be saved they must at least do some good otherwise how can they be saved? Yet they do not realize that such a thought is as foolish as presenting a piece of a new garment to put upon an old garment. The Bible does not tell us to improve ourselves, since the Lord has already done it all. Jesus Christ has borne our sins on the cross and there He said “It is finished.” He has completed the work and nothing is therefore left to be done. Today we do not need to do anything except to confess that our garment is torn, that we are corrupted and are unable to do any good, and to ask Him to give us a new garment. However, if you want to excel, you will have to do it repeatedly. You ought to know that aside from trusting the redemption which the Lord Jesus has accomplished once and for all, there is no other way of salvation. “No man rips a piece from a new garment and puts it upon an old garment or else he will rip the new, and also the piece from the new will not match with the old.” To tear the new means to destroy the finished work of Jesus Christ. Additionally, the new and the old will never agree. For instance, if you take a piece of a new, white garment and put it on an old, black garment, the difference in colors will be instantly noticeable. To mend something it requires a certain compatibility between materials. By placing a piece of a new garment on an old one, the disparity in colors will immediately reveal the wear and tear. This is like telling people how unfit things are. Let us be reminded that the salvation which God gives to us, as represented by a new garment, is totally different from our old garment. Are you thinking of filling in what you lack with the Lord Jesus? This is totally unacceptable. If you believe in the Lord Jesus, then you must accept a brand new garment. If you take only a little of the new garment, you will look even worse. Today we have a new garment, which is the righteousness of God. If you wholly accept the Lord, the righteousness of God will cover all your shame and nakedness. However, if you contemplate taking only a piece from the new garment, which is the righteousness of God, and putting it on your old garment, this will only serve to expose your own ugliness. The teaching of Jesus Christ is like unfinished cloth; therefore, it cannot save us. It is His finished work of redemption that saves us. Yet we cannot tear a piece from His garment of redemption to put on our ragged conduct. We can only take off completely what we consider our best conduct and put on the new garment of righteousness given by God. For God wants us to throw away our rags and to be clothed with His new garment. What man has is a ragged garment, but thank God for what He has is a new garment. There is no reason for man to refuse this new garment? Hallelujah! The redemption of Jesus Christ is sufficient for every person’s salvation. If any man is not saved, it is not because there is no new garment nor because he does not know how to mend his old garment but because he refuses to be clothed with the new garment. On the other hand, a person is saved not because he has good conduct, but because he believes and accepts the finished work of the Lord Jesus. Whether one is saved or not does not depend on his past as a good man or a bad man but entirely depends upon whether he accepts or rejects the redemption of the Lord. All who are willing to receive Jesus Christ shall be saved. “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.” (John 3:16) Hallelujah! This is a fact. The Son of God already died, and the new garment is also available. All you need is to be willing to put it on. Praise the Lord! The problem with salvation is not how valuable our conduct is but how valuable the cross of Calvary is. In this matter of salvation, our conduct has no merit at all; it’s the death of the Lord Jesus on the cross that is meritorious. The New Wine “Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.” (Matthew 9:17). The “Garment” points to the external work of the gospel, for it is visible to men. The “New wine” refers to the internal work of the gospel because it is invisible to men. The gospel of God includes two aspects: first, to make Christ our righteousness so that we may live before God in this righteousness. Nothing needs to be added because Christ has already become the righteousness of God; it is therefore impossible to add anything to it. Not because our good conduct has pleased God, but simply because Christ died and resurrected. Being in Christ, we are looked upon by God as acceptable to Him as Christ himself. We are saved not because we are different from other people, but because we are in Christ. Being in Christ, we can approach God. Having been clothed with Christ, we can live before God and please Him. The second aspect of the gospel is for Christ to live in us that we may live before the world. According to the spirit, we live before God; according to the flesh, we live in this world. “Garment” tells of how God gives us Christ and has made Him to be our righteousness so that we may live before God. “Wine” speaks of how God gives us Christ and has made Him to be our life and power that we may accept His control and by Him live before men. Some people complain, saying, “Indeed, I am saved and have received forgiveness of sins before God, but my daily life is still the same as before. What can I do about it?” Please remember that God has not only clothed you outwardly with a new garment in order to cover and adorn you, He has also put inside you a power like that of the new wine which will dissolve all the old things. We should know that salvation has this double aspect: that of the objective which is before God, and that of the subjective which is within us. In other words, there is justification on the one hand and regeneration on the other. It is absolutely impossible to be regenerated and not be justified, or justified without being regenerated. Justification obtains for us a new position before God, whereas regeneration gives us a new life. Some people pay attention only to justification without so much as considering this aspect of regeneration, yet other people overemphasise regeneration and overlook justification. Due to their misconception, none of these people realize that regeneration and justification co-occur, and they can hold such prejudiced views. Actually, justification and regeneration balance each other well. In the third chapter of the Gospel of John, the word “must” occurs several times. We will focus on two of them. In verse 7, “Do not marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born again.”(John 3:7) “And as Moses lifted the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted,” (John 3:14). The same word in Greek is used in both cases. What is said in verse 14 is objective, for the Lord Jesus is lifted that we may receive the forgiveness of sins and be justified. What is stated in verse 7 is subjective, as it promises us new life. Being justified, we have liberty before God; having been regenerated, we have a new life within us. Some people may speculate within themselves, thinking, “I am very much afraid to approach God because I do not know if He will save me or not.” They believe, won’t God say to me, ‘Depart from me, you wicked one!’ I am a sinner, I do not know whether God wants me or not.” To such people we would say: Do not be afraid, for the Lord Jesus has already come and has died for our sins. He has already satisfied God’s justice, and He has also been resurrected. Today, all who come to God through the Lord Jesus Christ shall be saved. The Lord himself has assured us that “Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God.” (John 3:18) Paul also declared that “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Acts 13:39). You who trust in the Lord today are justified. You ought to know that through Him you can come before God with a conscience free of fear because “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” (Romans 8:1) You know you are saved. Yet, you feel miserable because you want to do what is good, but you cannot carry it out. “For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out.” (Romans 7:18) You have seen changes in the lives of other believers, yet in yourself you see no change. You are saved as much as they are; why then are there changes in them but none in you? Why is your life not much different from what you were before? You cry over your defeats and weaknesses. You think over the matter of your salvation. You have to acknowledge that you are saved and that you have eternal life; but being the kind of person as you are, you ask yourself if you are really saved because you can hardly believe so. Therefore, you try hard er to do good, to pray, and to read the Bible more, and to discipline yourself more strictly in order to please God. You seem to see some results in three or five days, yet the effect is all in vain when measured by months or years. This is exactly what the Lord Jesus meant when He said we must not mend the old garment with a piece from the new garment; that after being saved, we ought to use the new wine, the power of this new life to overcome all outward entanglements. The new wine is put within us to give us new life and the power of living. All who are justified are regenerated. Whoever has the new garment also has the new wine. Hallelujah! God has already put this regenerated life in us; henceforth we are new men. The new wine is the power of the gospel. We have this power in us, causing us to live a victorious life. Now the question is, where is the new wine to be put? The New Wine-skins and the Old Wine-skins “Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.”(Matthew 9:17) Why should the new wine not be put into old wine-skins? (According to Jewish custom, wine is put into skins) It is because the new wine has tremendous power of expansion. It will burst the old wine-skin if it is put into it, and then the wine will be spilled. What is the meaning of the old wine-skins? Some people say that the old wine-skins represent us but this kind of interpretation is not correct. Since the old garment does not stand for us, how can the old wineskins represent us? We ought to consider the context of these words. As the old garment points to the so called self-righteousness of men, so the old wine-skins refers to our natural good conduct. This old wineskin is related to fasting in the preceding passage. Fasting enables us to boast that we are not like the tax-collector since we fast twice a week. What causes us to boast before God is the old wine-skins. Old wine-skins speaks of both the better conduct we consider ourselves as having had before we were saved as well as the good works which we may depend on after we are saved. As Christians, we may turn back like the Galatian believers and think of pleasing God by keeping the law. We try to rely on our own strength to obtain His favor. This is what Paul observed in the third chapter of Galatians: “Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3). All who begin with the Lord Jesus and then try to be perfected by themselves are putting new wine into old wine-skins. In the past to date, no one has been able to mix Christianity and Judaism and still preserve both. The result of such a mixture can only cause Christianity to be unlike Christianity and Judaism to be unlike Judaism. Both will lose their original flavor. God will not tolerate such a thing. The Roman church has combined Judaism with Christianity. On the one hand, they adopt the customs and rituals of the Old Covenant; on the other hand, they embrace the name of the New Covenant. Is this Christianity? No. Is this Judaism? The answer is equally no. Add Judaism to Christianity and the result is neither Judaism nor Christianity. The new wine can only be put into fresh wineskins. Only then can it be powerful and effective. The new wine must follow the principle of the New Covenant, and then it will please God. Having this new wine in you, you have a power within that can control you. If you are not saved, you will not have such an experience, and neither will you change. However, if you are saved, you will always sense within you a law that is in control of you. There was a mother who was very careful in speech, but she had a very talkative son. Whenever they visited their relatives, the mother would pull his sleeves to signal that he should stop talking because he had already said enough. Yet during the conversation, her son would talk constantly and completely ignore his mother’s pulling of his sleeve. How marvelous it is for a Christian that when he goes out alone with no one at his side and becomes too talkative, he feels within him a person pulling him, saying, That is enough. For if he continues to speak, he will be ungodly and unlike a Christian. As soon as he listens to the inner voice and stops talking, he experiences peace. What is this? This is the new wine. Can we put new wine into old wineskins? No, it is right to inscribe the words of the Bible upon our hearts, but to write them on the wall is like putting them into old wine-skins. In other words, this is an attempt to uphold the law through our own efforts. The law of the Old Covenant is external, while that of the New Covenant is internal. Here is the difference between the New Covenant and the Old. Just as the people under the Old Covenant could not, in themselves, keep the Ten Commandments, so too Christians under the New Covenant cannot keep such external commandments either. The Old Covenant is inscribed on stone tablets, the words of which we in ourselves have no power to keep; but the New Covenant is written upon the heart, giving us strength to keep it. Thank God, we do not need words written on paper to remind us. We instead have one who reminds us from within. The new wine cannot be put into old wine-skins. The latest wine must be put into fresh wine-skins. God has not commanded us to keep the outward law, but He does command us to keep the inward law. For the law within us is living and not dead. “For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death.”(Romans 8:2) This law is in us, and it enables us to keep the law of God. We have not only the new garment outside, but also the new wine inside. We have not only righteousness but also new life. The latest wine is put into fresh wine-skins, that we may live in the newness of life. The Old Wine “And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.” (Luke 5:39). This is the consensus of the world. All who have drunk the old wine will not desire the new. Yet, God will not give old wine to man to drink. The Jews rejected what the Lord Jesus gave to them because they had drunk too much of the old wine. How our minds, too, are drunk with old wine. We think that it will be well if we do well and improve ourselves. In actual fact, however, if a person drinks only the old wine, there is no new power, no real explosive power in him. If he does not drink the new wine, he will be powerless year after year. He who thinks of pleasing God with his own good conduct is following a futile path. Only by trusting in the Lord Jesus Christ and drinking the new wine can a person please God. Having studied these parables of the new and the old, we can now clearly understand that there is absolutely no way to mix up law and grace. Let us never for a moment try to mend our rags with the righteousness of Christ, but simply put on Christ. Let us never think that we have to do good after we are saved; let us simply trust Christ as our life and let Him live Himself out through us.

fields.title: Insights from the Parable of the Prodigal Son
fields.body_html:
